finding.claim: GET /users has no authentication or organization-ownership check, so any unauthenticated caller can list the id and name of users in any organization by supplying an arbitrary org value.
finding.source: req.query.org (db.js:9), unauthenticated HTTP query parameter on GET /users (db.js:8)
finding.sink: req.pg.query SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE org = $1 (db.js:9), response via res.json(rows) (db.js:10)

trace.note: Route app.get("/users") registered with no auth middleware
req.query.org passed as parameter $1 into the org filter; no check that the caller belongs to that org
All matching rows returned to the caller as JSON
app.listen applies no app-wide auth; no auth middleware is visible in this repo

finding.guards_checked: Parameterized query ($1) at db.js:9 blocks SQL injection but not authorization. No auth or ownership check on the route (db.js:8-11). No global middleware in db.js (db.js:1-23). Caveat: req.pg and any global middleware are defined outside this repo and could not be read; if they enforce auth, the finding does not hold.

verdict.guard_found: None in db.js. The route at db.js:8 has no auth middleware, and db.js:9 passes req.query.org straight into the query. The parameterized $1 at db.js:9 only blocks SQL injection, not an org-ownership bypass. Nothing else exists in the repo (Glob returns only db.js), so no global auth is visible.
verdict.reason: The route at db.js:8 is unauthenticated, req.query.org flows into the SELECT at db.js:9 with no ownership check, and rows are returned at db.js:10, so an anonymous caller can enumerate users of any org. The caveat is that req.pg (db.js:9) is never defined in this repo and an upstream proxy or middleware could enforce auth, but nothing in the code shown does.
